plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: In the wild, the poinsettia is a tall shrub or small tree, reaching 3–4 metres. Its fiery red bracts, which are modified leaves, flare out around tiny yellow-green flower clusters. The effect is like a scarlet starburst against the winter hillsides.
plants.bloomingSeason: December, as the short days and long nights of late autumn and early winter trigger flowering
plants.location: Native to Mexico and Central America, in seasonally dry forests and hillsides
plants.funFact: The showy 'petals' are not petals at all. They are leaves that change colour in response to long nights, and the true flowers are the tiny cup-shaped clusters at their centre.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: This glossy-leaved evergreen brightens the dull winter landscape with red, pink and white blooms. Its petals drift down one by one, leaving a soft carpet beneath the shrub.
plants.location: Native to Japan, and widely grown in gardens and parks there
plants.funFact: Sasanqua is easy to confuse with its cousin the tsubaki camellia. The giveaway is how the flowers fall: sasanqua petals shed individually, while tsubaki blooms drop whole.

plants.name: Ceratopetalum gummiferum
plants.description: In the sandstone gullies and coastal heaths around Sydney, this shrub produces airy sprays of tiny creamy-white flowers. As summer arrives, the star-shaped sepals swell and blush deep red, so the bush looks decorated for the holidays.
plants.bloomingSeason: November to December, with the red colour deepening through the Australian summer and fading by February
plants.location: Eastern Australia, especially the Hawkesbury Sandstone country around Sydney, New South Wales
plants.funFact: The red 'flowers' people notice are mainly enlarged sepals. The true petals stay tiny, at about 3 mm long, so the red display comes from the calyx, not the petals.
